source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics - Appendix & Glossary
attribution: From the "Common Core State Standards for MATHEMATICS" (Glossary, Tables 1-5)

terms.definition: Pairs of linked numerical observations.
terms.example: A list of heights and weights for each player on a football team.

terms.definition: A method of visually displaying a distribution of data values by using the median, quartiles, and extremes of the data set. A box shows the middle 50% of the data.
terms.seeAlso: First quartile, Median, Third quartile, Interquartile range

terms.definition: A fraction $A/B$ where $A$ and/or $B$ are fractions ($B$ nonzero).
A set of predefined steps applicable to a class of problems that gives the correct result in every case when the steps are carried out correctly.
Purposeful manipulations that may be chosen for specific problems, may not have a fixed order, and may be aimed at converting one problem into another.
Two plane or solid figures are congruent if one can be obtained from the other by a sequence of rigid motions (rotations, reflections, and translations).
A strategy for finding the number of objects in a group without having to count every member of the group.
terms.example: If a stack of books is known to have 8 books and 3 more are added to the top, it is not necessary to count the stack all over again; one can find the total by counting on—pointing to the top books and saying "eight," then counting on "nine, ten, eleven. There are eleven books now."

terms.definition: A transformation that moves each point along the ray through the point emanating from a fixed center, and multiplies its distance from the point by a common scale factor.
A method of visually displaying a distribution of data values where each data value is shown as a dot or mark above a number line.
A multi-digit number is expressed in expanded form when it is written as a sum of single-digit multiples of powers of ten.
For a random variable, the weighted average of its possible values, with weights given by their respective probabilities.
For a data set with median $M$, the first quartile is the median of the data values less than $M$.
terms.example: For the data set $\{1, 3, 6, 7, 10, 12, 14, 15, 22, 120\}$, the median is $11$. The data values less than $11$ are $\{1, 3, 6, 7, 10\}$. The median of these values is $6$; therefore, the first quartile is $6$.

terms.definition: A number expressible in the form $a/b$ where $a$ is a whole number and $b$ is a positive whole number. (The word fraction in these standards always refers to a non-negative number.)
For any number $a$, $a + 0 = 0 + a = a$.

A number expressible in the form $a$ or $-a$ for some whole number $a$. The set of integers includes positive whole numbers, negative whole numbers, and zero: $\{\dots, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\}$.
A measure of variation in a set of numerical data. The interquartile range is the distance between the first and third quartiles of the data set.
terms.example: For the data set $\{1, 3, 6, 7, 10, 12, 14, 15, 22, 120\}$, the first quartile is $6$ and the third quartile is $15$; the interquartile range is $15 - 6 = 9$.

terms.definition: A method of visually displaying a distribution of data values where each data value is shown as a dot or mark above a number line. Also known as a dot plot.
A measure of center in a set of numerical data, computed by adding the values in a list and then dividing by the number of values in the list.
A measure of variation in a set of numerical data, computed by adding the distances between each data value and the mean, then dividing by the number of data values.
terms.example: For the data set $\{2, 3, 6, 7, 10, 12, 14, 15, 22, 120\}$, the mean absolute deviation is $20$.

terms.definition: A measure of center in a set of numerical data. The median of a list of values is the value appearing at the center of a sorted version of the list—or the mean of the two central values, if the list contains an even number of values.
In the graph of a trigonometric function, the horizontal line halfway between its maximum and minimum values.
Standard situations categorized by Equal Groups, Arrays/Area, and Compare situations across Unknown Product, Group Size Unknown, and Number of Groups Unknown.
terms.seeAlso: Table 2: Common Multiplication and Division Situations

terms.definition: A diagram of the number line used to represent numbers and support reasoning about numbers. In non-negative coordinates, the line begins with $0$ and goes on indefinitely to the right with unit length equal to the distance between consecutive whole numbers.
A rate of change expressed as a percent.
terms.example: If a population grows from $50$ to $55$ in a year, it grew by $(55-50)/50 = 5/50 = 10\%$ per year.

terms.definition: A number between $0$ and $1$ used to quantify likelihood for processes that have uncertain outcomes (such as tossing a coin, selecting a person at random from a group of people, tossing a ball at a target, or testing for a medical condition).
The set of possible values of a random variable with a probability assigned to each.

A probability model is used to assign probabilities to outcomes of a chance process by examining the nature of the process. The set of all outcomes is called the sample space, and their probabilities sum to $1$.
Foundational mathematical truths governing equal expressions (Reflexive, Symmetric, Transitive, Addition, Subtraction, Multiplication, Division, and Substitution).
Mathematical properties that maintain inequality direction under addition, subtraction, positive scaling, and reversed direction under negative scaling.
Fundamental rules of arithmetic governing addition and multiplication (Associative, Commutative, Additive Identity, Multiplicative Identity, Inverses, and Distributive).
An assignment of a numerical value to each outcome in a sample space.
A relationship between two quantities where for every $a$ units of one quantity there are $b$ units of the other quantity. Often written $a:b$ or $a\text{ to }b$.
A quotient of two polynomials with a non-zero denominator.
A number expressible in the form $a/b$ or $-a/b$ for some whole number $a$ and some positive whole number $b$. The rational numbers include the integers.
A number from the continuum of points on a line. The set of real numbers includes all rational and irrational numbers.
The decimal form of a rational number where a sequence of one or more digits repeats indefinitely without terminating.
In a probability model for a random process, a list of the individual outcomes that are to be considered.
A graphic display of bivariate data on a coordinate plane with one variable on each axis.
A rigid motion (rotation, reflection, translation) followed by a dilation.
A measure of the spread of a set of data from its mean. It is the square root of the variance: $\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i - \mu)^2}$.
A drawing that looks like a segment of tape, used to illustrate number relationships. Also known as a strip diagram, bar model, fraction strip, or length model.
A decimal is called terminating if its repeating digit is $0$ (for example, $0.25000\dots = 0.25$).
For a data set with median $M$, the third quartile is the median of the data values greater than $M$.
terms.example: For the data set $\{2, 3, 6, 7, 10, 12, 14, 15, 22, 120\}$, the median is $11$. The data values greater than $11$ are $\{12, 14, 15, 22, 120\}$. The median of these values is $15$; therefore, the third quartile is $15$.

terms.definition: If the length of object $A$ is greater than the length of object $B$, and the length of object $B$ is greater than the length of object $C$, then the length of object $A$ is greater than the length of object $C$. Symbolically, if $A > B$ and $B > C$, then $A > C$.
A probability model which assigns equal probability to all outcomes.
A quantity with magnitude and direction in the plane or in space, represented by an arrow from an initial point to a terminal point.
A tape diagram, number line diagram, or area model used to visually represent fraction operations and equivalence.

tables.title: Common Addition and Subtraction Situations
tables.description: Classification of addition and subtraction situations across problem types and unknown positions, directly from Table 1 of the CCSS Mathematics Glossary.

rows.resultUnknown:
Two bunnies sat on the grass. Three more bunnies hopped there. How many bunnies are on the grass now?
$$2 + 3 = ?$$
rows.changeUnknown:
Two bunnies were sitting on the grass. Some more bunnies hopped there. Then there were five bunnies. How many bunnies hopped over?
$$2 + ? = 5$$
rows.startUnknown:
Some bunnies were sitting on the grass. Three more bunnies hopped there. Then there were five bunnies. How many bunnies were on the grass before?
$$? + 3 = 5$$

rows.resultUnknown:
Five apples were on the table. I ate two apples. How many apples are on the table now?
$$5 - 2 = ?$$
rows.changeUnknown:
Five apples were on the table. I ate some apples. Then there were three apples. How many apples did I eat?
$$5 - ? = 3$$
rows.startUnknown:
Some apples were on the table. I ate two apples. Then there were three apples. How many apples were on the table before?
$$? - 2 = 3$$

rows.resultUnknown:
Three red apples and two green apples are on the table. How many apples are on the table?
$$3 + 2 = ?$$
rows.changeUnknown:
Five apples are on the table. Three are red and the rest are green. How many apples are green?
$$3 + ? = 5, \quad 5 - 3 = ?$$
rows.startUnknown:
Grandma has five flowers. How many can she put in her red vase and how many in her blue vase?
$$5 = 0 + 5, \ 5 = 1 + 4, \ 5 = 2 + 3, \dots$$

rows.resultUnknown:
("How many more?") Lucy has two apples. Julie has five apples. How many more apples does Julie have than Lucy?
("How many fewer?") Lucy has two apples. Julie has five apples. How many fewer apples does Lucy have than Julie?
$$2 + ? = 5, \quad 5 - 2 = ?$$
rows.changeUnknown:
(Version with "more") Julie has 3 more apples than Lucy. Lucy has 2 apples. How many apples does Julie have?
(Version with "fewer") Lucy has 3 fewer apples than Julie. Lucy has 2 apples. How many apples does Julie have?
$$2 + 3 = ?$$
rows.startUnknown:
(Version with "more") Julie has 3 more apples than Lucy. Julie has 5 apples. How many apples does Lucy have?
(Version with "fewer") Lucy has 3 fewer apples than Julie. Julie has 5 apples. How many apples does Lucy have?
$$5 - 3 = ?, \quad ? + 3 = 5$$

tables.title: Common Multiplication and Division Situations
tables.description: Classification of multiplication and division situations across Equal Groups, Arrays/Area, and Compare situations, directly from Table 2 of the CCSS Mathematics Glossary.
headers: Group Size Unknown ("How many in each group?")
Number of Groups Unknown ("How many groups?")

rows.unknownProduct:
There are $3$ bags with $6$ plums in each bag. How many plums are there in all?
Measurement example: You need $3$ lengths of string, each $6$ inches long. How much string will you need altogether?
$$3 \times 6 = ?$$
rows.groupSizeUnknown:
If $18$ plums are shared equally into $3$ bags, then how many plums will be in each bag?
Measurement example: You have $18$ inches of string, which you will cut into $3$ equal pieces. How long will each piece of string be?
$$3 \times ? = 18, \quad 18 \div 3 = ?$$
rows.numGroupsUnknown:
If $18$ plums are to be packed $6$ to a bag, then how many bags are needed?
Measurement example: You have $18$ inches of string, which you will cut into pieces that are $6$ inches long. How many pieces of string will you have?
$$? \times 6 = 18, \quad 18 \div 6 = ?$$

rows.unknownProduct:
There are $3$ rows of apples with $6$ apples in each row. How many apples are there?
Area example: What is the area of a $3\text{ cm} \times 6\text{ cm}$ rectangle?
$$3 \times 6 = ?$$
rows.groupSizeUnknown:
If $18$ apples are arranged into $3$ equal rows, how many apples will be in each row?
Area example: A rectangle has area $18\text{ cm}^2$. If one side is $3\text{ cm}$ long, how long is a side that is perpendicular to it?
$$3 \times ? = 18, \quad 18 \div 3 = ?$$
rows.numGroupsUnknown:
If $18$ apples are arranged into equal rows of $6$ apples, how many rows will there be?
Area example: A rectangle has area $18\text{ cm}^2$. If one side is $6\text{ cm}$ long, how long is a side that is perpendicular to it?
$$? \times 6 = 18, \quad 18 \div 6 = ?$$

rows.unknownProduct:
A blue hat costs $\$6$. A red hat costs $3$ times as much as the blue hat. How much does the red hat cost?
Measurement example: A rubber band is $6\text{ cm}$ long. How long will the rubber band be when it is stretched to be $3$ times as long?
$$3 \times 6 = ?$$
rows.groupSizeUnknown:
A red hat costs $\$18$ and that is $3$ times as much as a blue hat costs. How much does a blue hat cost?
Measurement example: A rubber band is stretched to be $18\text{ cm}$ long and that is $3$ times as long as it was at first. How long was the rubber band at first?
$$3 \times ? = 18, \quad 18 \div 3 = ?$$
rows.numGroupsUnknown:
A red hat costs $\$18$ and a blue hat costs $\$6$. How many times as much does the red hat cost as the blue hat?
Measurement example: A rubber band was $6\text{ cm}$ long at first. Now it is stretched to be $18\text{ cm}$ long. How many times as long is the rubber band now as it was at first?
$$? \times 6 = 18, \quad 18 \div 6 = ?$$

tables.title: The Properties of Operations
tables.description: Here $a$, $b$, and $c$ stand for arbitrary numbers in a given number system. The properties of operations apply to the rational number system, the real number system, and the complex number system.

rows.statement: For every $a$ there exists $-a$ such that $$a + (-a) = (-a) + a = 0$$
$$(a \times b) \times c = a \times (b \times c)$$
$$a \times b = b \times a$$
$$a \times 1 = 1 \times a = a$$
For every $a \neq 0$ there exists $1/a$ such that $$a \times 1/a = 1/a \times a = 1$$

rows.property: Distributive property of multiplication over addition
rows.statement: $$a \times (b + c) = a \times b + a \times c$$

tables.title: The Properties of Equality
tables.description: Here $a$, $b$, and $c$ stand for arbitrary numbers in the rational, real, or complex number systems.

rows.statement: If $a = b$, then $$b = a$$
If $a = b$ and $b = c$, then $$a = c$$
If $a = b$, then $$a + c = b + c$$
If $a = b$, then $$a - c = b - c$$
If $a = b$, then $$a \times c = b \times c$$
If $a = b$ and $c \neq 0$, then $$a \div c = b \div c$$
If $a = b$, then $b$ may be substituted for $a$ in any expression containing $a$.

tables.title: The Properties of Inequality
tables.description: Here $a$, $b$, and $c$ stand for arbitrary real numbers.

rows.statement: Exactly one of $a < b$, $a = b$, or $a > b$ is true.
If $a > b$ and $b > c$, then $$a > c$$
If $a > b$, then $$b < a$$
If $a > b$, then $$-a < -b$$
If $a > b$, then $$a + c > b + c$$
If $a > b$, then $$a - c > b - c$$
If $a > b$ and $c > 0$, then $$a \times c > b \times c$$
If $a > b$ and $c < 0$, then $$a \times c < b \times c$$
If $a > b$ and $c > 0$, then $$a \div c > b \div c$$
If $a > b$ and $c < 0$, then $$a \div c < b \div c$$
